clinician.trajectory_summary: An 86-year-old Japanese woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, angina pectoris, and chronic kidney disease presented with 12 hours of sudden-onset abdominal pain. On admission, she had severe metabolic lactic acidosis (pH 7.110, lactate 9.1 mmol/L), leukocytosis, marked inflammatory signs, and markedly elevated serum phosphate (14.4 mg/dL) disproportionate to her renal dysfunction—all indicating acute mesenteric ischemia with tissue damage. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed dilated colon and small intestine with fluid but no complete obstruction, free air, ascites, or classic ischemic signs (no bowel wall enhancement loss, pneumatosis intestinalis, hepatic portal venous gas, or wall thickening). Upon admission, she had signs of shock (cold limbs, mottled skin, O2 saturation 98% on 4L oxygen). One hour after admission, her systolic blood pressure acutely decreased from 139 to 60 mmHg and she went into shock. Six hours after admission, emergency surgery was performed, revealing ileum and whole colon (except sigmoid) were discontinuously necrotic despite pulsation of the superior mesenteric artery—the pathognomonic finding for NOMI. Ileal resection, subtotal colectomy, and jejunostomy were performed (residual jejunal length 120 cm). The patient recovered after surgery, and her serum phosphate level immediately returned to normal range.

On admission, she had severe metabolic lactic acidosis (pH 7.110, lactate 9.1 mmol/L), leukocytosis, marked inflammatory signs, and markedly elevated serum phosphate (14.4 mg/dL) disproportionate to her renal dysfunction—all indicating acute mesenteric ischemia with tissue damage. Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed dilated colon and small intestine with fluid but no complete obstruction, free air, ascites, or classic ischemic signs (no bowel wall enhancement loss, pneumatosis intestinalis, hepatic portal venous gas, or wall thickening). Upon admission, she had signs of shock (cold limbs, mottled skin, O2 saturation 98% on 4L oxygen). One hour after admission, her systolic blood pressure acutely decreased from 139 to 60 mmHg and she went into shock. Six hours after admission, emergency surgery was performed, revealing ileum and whole colon (except sigmoid) were discontinuously necrotic despite pulsation of the superior mesenteric artery—the pathognomonic finding for NOMI. Ileal resection, subtotal colectomy, and jejunostomy were performed (residual jejunal length 120 cm). The patient recovered after surgery, and her serum phosphate level immediately returned to normal range.
